problems.body: A parking lot has 6 rows with 8 cars in each row. How many cars?

commonErrors.feedback: 14 adds 6 + 8 — but every row holds a whole group of 8. Six groups of 8 multiply.
68 glues the digits side by side. The rows are equal groups: count 8, six times.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Six equal rows of 8: run the fact 6 × 8.

hints: Rows are equal groups — same count in every one.
Six groups of eight is the fact 6 × 8.
explanationVariants: 6 rows × 8 cars = 48 — six equal groups of eight.
Skip-count a row at a time: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48 cars.

problems.body: 56 stickers are shared equally among 7 friends. How many does each friend get?

commonErrors.feedback: 49 took 7 away once — but sharing splits ALL 56 into 7 equal piles, not one handout.
392 multiplied 56 × 7. Sharing goes the other way: the total gets divided.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Total first: 56 split into 7 equal piles is 56 ÷ 7.

hints: The total (56) is known — it gets split.
explanationVariants: Deal them out: 7 piles grow together and hit 56 when each pile holds 8.

problems.body: Just the fact — fast and sure.

commonErrors.feedback: 13 adds 4 + 9. Four GROUPS of nine multiply.
49 glues the digits. The fact counts 9 four times: 36.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count 9 four times, or use 4 × 10 − 4.

hints: Nine is one less than ten.
explanationVariants: 4 × 9 = 40 − 4 = 36 — ride the tens fact, then step back one group.
Nines check: 3 + 6 = 9. The digits of a nines answer sum to nine.

problems.body: A coach has 9 balls and packs 9 balls into each bag. How many bags does she fill?

commonErrors.feedback: 9 answers with the number itself — but 9 ÷ 9 asks how many groups of 9 fit inside 9: exactly one.
Zero bags would mean no group fits — yet one full group of 9 is sitting right there.
18 added the nines. The 9 balls form groups OF 9: just one.

widget.fallbackFeedback: How many 9s fit in 9? One whole group, exactly.

hints: The total and the group size are the same number.
How many groups of 9 fit inside 9?
One group uses ALL the balls.
explanationVariants: 9 ÷ 9 = 1 — a number divided by itself makes exactly one group.
Check with the fact family: 1 × 9 = 9, so 9 ÷ 9 = 1.

problems.body: Ben buys 3 packs of 10 pencils, then gives 4 pencils away. How many does he keep?

commonErrors.feedback: 30 is the first pile — the buy. The give-away hasn't happened yet: subtract 4.
34 ADDED the give-away. Pencils that leave come off the pile.
18 subtracted inside a pack first ((10 − 4) × 3) — but the 4 leave the WHOLE pile once, after the packs are counted.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Build the pile (3 × 10), then subtract the 4 that leave.

hints: Two steps: build first, then change.
explanationVariants: 3 × 10 = 30, then 30 − 4 = 26 — build the pile, then let the give-away change it.
Say the middle pile out loud: 'thirty pencils.' Only then take the 4 away.

problems.body: The famous hard one.

commonErrors.feedback: 54 is the 6 × 9 answer sneaking in — these two facts love to swap. Seven 8s land on 56.
15 adds 7 + 8. Seven GROUPS of eight multiply.
78 glues the digits. Count eight, seven times.

hints: There's a counting trick hiding in the digits.
Say it: five, six, seven, eight…
56 = 7 × 8 — the answer leads right into the fact.
explanationVariants: 5, 6, 7, 8 — read as 56 = 7 × 8. The fact spells itself.
Build it from a friend: 7 × 4 = 28, and 8 is double 4, so double 28: 56.

problems.body: Same total, different view.

options.feedback: The flip! 5 rows of 7 and 7 rows of 5 are the same array turned sideways: 35 either way.
Adding gives 12 — that's one 5 and one 7 meeting once, not five whole groups of seven.
75 glues the digits together. The × sign means five GROUPS of seven: 35.
Division splits — it undoes multiplying. The flip that keeps the value is swapping the factors: 7 × 5.

hints: Turn the array sideways — did the dot count change?
Swapping the factors never changes the product.
explanationVariants: 5 × 7 and 7 × 5 are one array viewed two ways — 35 dots either way.
Multiplication commutes: the order of factors never changes the product.

problems.body: Undo the multiplication.

commonErrors.feedback: 36 subtracted 6 once — division asks how many WHOLE 6s fit in 42.
48 added instead. Dividing splits the 42 into groups of 6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Which times-6 fact reaches 42?

explanationVariants: 42 ÷ 6 = 7 because 6 × 7 = 42 — same family, opposite door.
Skip-count 6s and count your steps: seven hops reach 42.

problems.body: A baker makes 5 trays of 6 muffins, then eats 2 warm ones. How many are left to sell?

commonErrors.feedback: 30 is the full bake — before the baker's snack. Two muffins are gone.
32 ADDED the eaten muffins. Eaten muffins leave the pile.
20 took 2 off every tray ((6 − 2) × 5) — but only 2 muffins total were eaten, once.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Bake first (5 × 6), then subtract the 2 eaten.

hints: Build the bake, then change it.
explanationVariants: 5 × 6 = 30, then 30 − 2 = 28 — the snack comes off the whole bake, not each tray.
Middle pile out loud: 'thirty muffins,' then two disappear: 28.

problems.body: Find the hidden factor.

commonErrors.feedback: 48 subtracted 6 from 54 — but the blank is a FACTOR: how many 6s build 54?
6 × 8 = 48, one group short. One more 6 lands exactly on 54.

widget.fallbackFeedback: How many 6s stack up to 54?

hints: The blank asks how many 6s make 54.
explanationVariants: 6 × 9 = 54, so the blank is 9 — division in disguise.
Nines check: 5 + 4 = 9, a fingerprint of the nine times table.

problems.body: Skip-counting by 4: 4, 8, 12, … What is the 7th number you say?

commonErrors.feedback: 24 is the 6th stop — one hop short. Keep counting: each number is one more 4.
32 is the 8th stop — one hop too far. Count your hops as you go.
16 is only the 4th stop. Track hops and value separately: 7 hops of 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Seven hops of 4 is the fact 7 × 4.

hints: Each number in the count is one more group of 4.
explanationVariants: The 7th skip-count lands on 7 × 4 = 28 — counting position IS the factor.
March it out: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28 — seven stops.

problems.body: Eight groups with nothing in them.

commonErrors.feedback: 8 kept the number — but 8 × 0 means eight groups holding NOTHING. Eight empty bags carry zero.
80 treated the 0 as a place-shift badge — that's ×10's job. Times ZERO empties everything.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Eight bags, zero in each: how much total?

hints: Picture 8 bags with 0 marbles in each.
Any number of empty groups holds nothing.
explanationVariants: 8 × 0 = 0 — eight groups of nothing is still nothing.
Zero is multiplication's eraser: any factor times 0 collapses to 0.

problems.body: Divide with the table you know.

commonErrors.feedback: 7 × 8 = 56 — close, but 7 short of 63. One more group of 7 lands exactly.
56 subtracted 7 once. Division counts how many WHOLE 7s fill 63.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Which times-7 fact hits 63 exactly?

hints: Ask it as a missing factor: 7 × ? = 63.
explanationVariants: Nines check on 63: 6 + 3 = 9 — the nine family signs its work.

problems.body: You already know 6 × 4 = 24. Use it!

commonErrors.feedback: 32 added 8 to 24 — but 8 isn't one more than 4, it's DOUBLE. Double the whole answer.
28 added just 4. Going from ×4 to ×8 doubles every group's size: 24 doubles to 48.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 8 is double 4, so 6 × 8 is double 6 × 4.

hints: Doubling one factor doubles the product.
explanationVariants: Break the 8: 6 × 8 = 6 × 4 + 6 × 4 — two copies of a fact you own.

problems.body: The biggest square on the table.

commonErrors.feedback: 18 adds 9 + 9. Nine GROUPS of nine multiply.
72 is 8 × 9 — one group of 9 short of the square.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use 9 × 10 = 90, then step one 9 back.

hints: 90 is one group of 9 too many.
explanationVariants: 9 × 9 = 90 − 9 = 81 — the tens shortcut with one step back.
Nines check: 8 + 1 = 9. Every nines answer's digits sum to nine.

problems.body: 32 kids need seats. Each table seats 4. How many tables?

commonErrors.feedback: 28 subtracted one table's worth. The question asks how many WHOLE tables of 4 the 32 kids fill.
128 multiplied 32 × 4 — that would seat a school! The 32 gets split into 4s.
36 added a table's worth. Splitting a total is division: 32 ÷ 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Total first: 32 split into groups of 4.

hints: The total (32) is known and gets split.
Groups of 4: how many fit in 32?
explanationVariants: 32 ÷ 4 = 8 tables — because 8 × 4 = 32.
Seat them in fours and count tables: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32 — eight tables.

problems.body: Tickets cost $6 each. Maya buys 5 and pays with $40. How much change?

commonErrors.feedback: 30 is the COST of the tickets — step one done. The change is what's left of her 40.
70 ADDED cost to payment. Change comes back: 40 minus the cost.
34 subtracted one ticket. All five tickets cost 5 × 6 first — subtract that whole cost.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Cost first (5 × 6), then 40 minus that cost.

hints: Two steps: total cost, then change.
explanationVariants: Guard it: the change must be smaller than the 40 she handed over — 10 fits, 70 can't.

problems.body: Families stick together.

widget.prompt: Which fact belongs to the same family as 3 × 8 = 24?

options.feedback: Same three numbers, opposite door — the division undoes the multiplication.
Adding brings in a NEW number (32). Fact families reuse the same three: 3, 8, 24.
The total leads a division — 8 split into 3s can't grow to 24. The family's division starts from 24.
11 isn't in this family at all. The family's three members are 3, 8, and 24, linked by × and ÷.

hints: A fact family reuses the same three numbers.
Division in the family starts from the total, 24.
explanationVariants: 3 × 8 = 24 and 24 ÷ 8 = 3 share the same three numbers — one builds, one splits.
Every multiplication fact hides two divisions: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 and 24 ÷ 3 = 8.

problems.body: One more from the eights.

commonErrors.feedback: 40 subtracted 8 once. Division counts how many whole 8s fill 48.
8 × 7 = 56 — that overshoots 48 by a whole group. One fewer 8 lands exactly.

explanationVariants: Halve twice, sort of: 48 ÷ 2 = 24, ÷ 2 = 12… that's ÷4. One more halving (÷8): 6.

problems.body: A garden has 7 rows of 7 plants. A frost kills 5 plants. How many survive?

commonErrors.feedback: 49 is the garden before the frost — the 5 lost plants still need to come off.
54 ADDED the frost's damage. Killed plants leave the count.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Garden first (7 × 7), then subtract the 5 lost.

hints: Build the garden, then let the frost change it.
explanationVariants: 7 × 7 = 49, then 49 − 5 = 44 survivors.
Middle pile out loud: 'forty-nine plants' — then frost takes five: 44.

problems.body: 4 boxes hold 7 crayons each, and 3 loose crayons sit on the desk.

widget.prompt: Build one expression for ALL the crayons.

commonBuilds.feedback: The minus sends the loose crayons AWAY — but they're on the desk, part of the total. They join with +.
4 + 7 counts one box-count and one crayon-count meeting once. The boxes are equal groups — they multiply first.

widget.missFeedback: Equal groups first (4 × 7), then the loose 3 join the pile.

hints: The loose 3 simply join the total.
explanationVariants: 4 × 7 = 28 boxed crayons, plus 3 loose: 31 in all.
The flip 7 × 4 + 3 builds the same pile — factor order never matters.

problems.body: Spiders have 8 legs. How many legs on 7 spiders?

commonErrors.feedback: 15 adds 7 + 8 — one spider meets one leg-count. Seven whole spiders each bring 8 legs.
78 glues the digits. Count 8 legs, seven times over.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Seven groups of 8 legs: 7 × 8.

hints: Each spider is a group of 8.
explanationVariants: 7 × 8 = 56 legs — seven equal groups of eight.
Double-double-double: 7 → 14 → 28 → 56. Doubling three times is the same as ×8.

problems.body: Dividing by 4 the sneaky way: halve, then halve again.

commonErrors.feedback: 40 halved just once — that's 80 ÷ 2. Dividing by 4 needs the second halving.
76 subtracted 4. Division splits 80 into four equal parts.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Half of 80, then half again.

explanationVariants: 80 ÷ 4: halve to 40, halve again to 20.
Check by building back: 4 × 20 = 80 — the family agrees.

problems.body: A steady classic.

commonErrors.feedback: 13 adds 6 + 7. Six GROUPS of seven multiply.
36 is 6 × 6 — one group of 6 short. One more 6 reaches 42.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Build from 6 × 6 = 36, then one more 6.

explanationVariants: 6 × 7 = 6 × 6 + 6 = 36 + 6 = 42 — one step past the square.

problems.body: A book has 9 chapters of 10 pages each. Mia has read 30 pages. How many pages are left?

commonErrors.feedback: 90 is the whole book — Mia's 30 read pages haven't come off yet.
120 ADDED her reading to the book. Pages already read come OFF what's left.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Book first (9 × 10), then subtract the 30 read.

explanationVariants: In tens: 9 tens minus 3 tens is 6 tens — 60 pages.

problems.body: Leo says 6 × 9 = 45. Can you bust it without computing?

widget.prompt: What does one glance tell you?

options.label: Busted — an even number times anything stays even, and 45 is odd
options.feedback: The 6 makes every multiple of it even. 45 is odd, so it can't be 6 × anything. (It's 54.)

options.label: It's fine — 45 is a big enough number
options.feedback: Size alone isn't the test — 45 IS in the right neighborhood. Its ODDNESS is what betrays it: even × anything stays even.

options.label: You can't tell without multiplying it out
options.feedback: Parity tells instantly: 6 is even, so 6 × 9 must be even. 45 fails before any multiplying.

options.label: Busted — nines answers always end in 9
options.feedback: That rule isn't real (18, 27, 36…). The real one-glance rule here: an even factor forces an even answer.

hints: Look at the factor 6 — odd or even?
explanationVariants: 6 is even, so 6 × 9 must be even — 45 is odd, busted. The true answer is 54.
Nines check too: 4 + 5 = 9 fits, but parity overrules — both tests must pass, and evenness fails.

problems.body: Fours, backwards.

commonErrors.feedback: 32 subtracted 4 once. Division counts the whole 4s inside 36.
4 × 8 = 32 — one group of 4 short. One more 4 lands exactly on 36.

explanationVariants: Halve twice: 36 → 18 → 9.

problems.body: Same numbers, opposite jobs.

widget.prompt: Sort each story by the math it needs.

items.label: 6 bags with 3 apples in each — how many apples?
items.feedback: The total is unknown and being built from 6 equal groups: 6 × 3 = 18.

items.label: 18 apples, 3 to a basket — how many baskets?
items.feedback: The total (18) is known and gets split into 3s: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 baskets.

items.label: 3 rows of 6 chairs — how many chairs?
items.feedback: Equal rows build a total: 3 × 6 — the flip of 6 × 3, same 18.

items.label: 18 kids split into 3 equal teams — how big is each team?
items.feedback: The 18 is given and gets shared into 3 teams: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 per team.

widget.missFeedback: Find each story's total: unknown and growing → multiply; known and splitting → divide.
widget.successFeedback: Two build, two split — the total's job picks the operation every time.

hints: Find the total in each story.
explanationVariants: Stories that BUILD a total multiply; stories that SPLIT a known total divide.
6 × 3 = 18 and 18 ÷ 3 = 6 are one fact family telling two kinds of story.

problems.body: Ten groups, one shift.

commonErrors.feedback: 17 adds 10 + 7. Ten GROUPS of seven multiply.
107 glued the numbers. ×10 shifts the 7 one place left, and a 0 holds the ones: 70.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Times ten slides a digit one place up.

hints: ×10 is a place-value shift, not a gluing.
The 7 slides left; 0 holds the ones spot.
explanationVariants: 10 × 7 = 70 — the 7 shifts from ones to tens.
Count it: ten 7s is seven 10s (the flip), and seven tens read as 70.

problems.body: A class of 24 kids splits into teams of 4. Each team gets 2 balls. How many balls?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 is the number of TEAMS — the middle pile. Each of those teams still collects 2 balls.
48 multiplied 24 × 2 — that gives every KID two balls. The balls go to teams, so count teams first.
8 mixed the middle numbers. Teams first (24 ÷ 4 = 6), then 6 teams × 2 balls.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Teams first (24 ÷ 4), then 2 balls per team.

hints: Each of those teams takes 2 balls.
explanationVariants: 24 ÷ 4 = 6 teams; 6 × 2 = 12 balls.
Say the middle pile: 'six teams' — then the balls count 2 six times.
